title: Extreme Heat Is Crushing India's Workers: Lost Wages, Broken Bodies, and a Crisis With No Safety Net
excerpt: A new global report warns that heat stress could erase nearly 24 workdays per year for outdoor workers in South Asia by 2030, while India's garment factory study finds 87% of workers suffering heat-related symptoms.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Heat stress may cause South Asian workers to lose 24 workdays annually by 2030, impacting incomes.
  • 87% of garment workers in India report heat-related symptoms, including headaches and dizziness.
  • Over 90% of India's workforce lacks paid leave and health insurance, worsening heat impacts.
  • Annual medical spending in South Asia has increased 830% since 2000 due to climate-related health costs.

  • Heat stress could cause workers in South Asia to lose nearly 24 workdays per year by 2030, cutting incomes for millions in the informal economy
  • A HeatWatch-TISS study of India's garment factories found 87% of workers suffer heat-related symptoms including headaches, dizziness, and muscle cramps
  • Over 90% of India's workforce operates in the informal sector without paid leave, health insurance, or income protection during extreme heat
  • Annual per capita out-of-pocket medical spending in South Asia has surged 830% since 2000 as climate-related health costs mount

The Human Cost of Rising Temperatures

As India endures another punishing summer, a new global report from Berlin-based think tank adelphi reveals the staggering economic toll of extreme heat on the world's poorest workers. South Asian agriculture and construction workers could lose nearly 24 workdays per year by 2030 because of heat stress, the report warns, cutting incomes for millions of households already living without safety nets.

The report, "Heat, Health and the Increasing Costs of Living," analyses the relationship between heat, health, and living costs across eight countries including India, Brazil, France, and Nigeria. Its findings for South Asia are particularly alarming: annual working-hour losses are projected to increase from 4.24% to 4.84% across all sectors, with the hardest hit being informal workers who lack paid leave, health insurance, and income protection.

> **"Annual per capita out-of-pocket medical spending in South Asia has surged more than 830% since 2000."**

Inside India's Garment Factories

A separate study by HeatWatch and the Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) puts a human face on the crisis. The report, "Breaking Point: Heat and the Garment Floor," reveals how extreme heat is endangering the lives of India's garment workers, most of whom are women.

The findings are stark: 87% of workers reported heat-related symptoms including headaches, dizziness, and muscle cramps. Workers described lying on factory bathroom floors to get a few minutes of respite from the heat. Machines operating at 90 degrees Celsius amplify temperatures on shop floors where 80% of workstations have no air movement.

"The findings show that heat stress is not just an environmental crisis — it is a labour rights emergency. As temperatures rise, women workers face the brunt of production pressures, lost incomes, and worsening health."

— Apekshita Varshney, Founder, HeatWatch

The Numbers Behind the Suffering

The TISS study documented conditions that would be unimaginable in most developed economies. Among garment workers surveyed, 78.3% faced difficulty getting permission to use toilets, 36.5% said drinking water often ran out or was unclean, and 78% skipped breaks to meet production targets, showing nearly double the stress levels of those who took breaks.

Among women workers, 96.8% reported burning sensations during urination and 92.6% experienced disruptions to their menstrual cycles. These are not statistics from decades past; they describe conditions in factories today that produce garments for global brands.

A Workforce Without Protection

India's vast informal sector, encompassing over 90% of its workforce, bears the brunt of extreme heat. Labourers in construction, street vending, factories, and agriculture toil under relentless sun, while others battle stifling heat indoors. The 2024 heatwave claimed 143 lives and left over 41,000 suffering from suspected heatstroke between March and June, according to the Health Ministry.

Dr. Das, Director at the National Institute of Occupational Health, captures the impossible choice workers face: "It is clear that workers will not prioritise their health over their livelihoods during these extremely hot days, as this will lead to loss of wages and that is something they cannot afford."

The Financial Squeeze

The crisis extends beyond lost wages. Annual per capita out-of-pocket medical spending in South Asia has surged more than 830% since 2000. In some countries studied, nearly 80% of total health expenditure is paid directly by households. As heat intensifies and health costs rise, families already facing climate-related income losses are being pushed deeper into financial hardship.

Looking Ahead

The National Institute of Occupational Health has developed a nine-step plan integrating worker, employer, and government efforts to minimise heat stress. But unions and activists say most recommendations are commonsense ideas that workers already follow, and criticise the lack of labour inspections to enforce factory conditions.

For the Indian diaspora, these findings underscore the human cost of the climate crisis in their home country. As temperatures continue to rise, the gap between India's economic ambitions and the reality faced by its 500 million informal workers will only widen without systemic intervention.
